The motet is a polyphonic vocal composition on a sacred Latin text, originating in the medieval period and reaching its height during the Renaissance, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Unlike the mass, which sets fixed liturgical texts, the motet is a flexible form that could celebrate saints, mark feast days, or express personal devotion. It stands as the apex of Renaissance polyphonic craft, where multiple voice-parts interweave in intricate counterpoint.

The motet evolved from the organum of medieval cathedrals, where singers added new text and melody above existing liturgical chant. By the Renaissance, it had become a completely original polyphonic composition. Motets are almost always unaccompanied vocal music, sung a cappella, set to Latin sacred texts. The text can be a verse from the Bible, a liturgical antiphon, or a poetic meditation on faith.

Structurally, motets typically have four to six voice-parts that often enter one by one in imitative counterpoint. Each voice states a melodic idea and other voices echo or combine with it—a technique perfected in the Renaissance. Major Renaissance motet composers include Josquin des Prez, the Franco-Flemish master living circa 1450 to 1521; Orlando di Lasso, living from 1530 to 1594 and incredibly prolific; and Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the Italian master living from 1525 to 1594.

Palestrina's motets exemplify the clarity and flowing counterpoint that defined late Renaissance style. His work was seen as the model for liturgically correct polyphonic music and influenced centuries of church music composition. The motet was the primary form for ambitious sacred polyphonic composition before the Baroque era elevated the mass and the cantata to prominence. Through its sophisticated treatment of text and music, the motet remains one of the highest achievements of Renaissance composition.
